title: Quattuor aetates. Gigantes
titleEn: The Four Ages, and the Giants — Metamorphoses I.89–162
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: These lines give Ovid's account of the four ages of the world, told near the beginning of the Metamorphoses, just after the creation and the making of man. The race of gold lives under Saturn with no law, no courts, no ships, no farming and no war; the silver race comes in under Jupiter, and with it the four seasons, houses and the plough; bronze is harsher but not yet criminal; and iron brings sailing, land-surveying, mining, war, and the breaking of every bond between guest and host, husband and wife, father and son, until Astraea, the maiden Justice, leaves the earth altogether. The passage then closes with the Giants heaping mountains to storm heaven, Jupiter's thunderbolt, and a new race of men grown out of their blood — violent, as their origin would suggest. The scheme of metal ages comes from Hesiod, but the furniture is Roman throughout: bronze law-tablets, a 'iudex' to be feared, a surveyor's boundary-line, the trumpet and horn of the legions. Latin verse lets sentences run straight across the line-breaks, so the unit you tap often begins or ends in mid-line; the line numbers are the standard way of citing the poem. There is no text-to-speech for Latin here — the reading is by eye.

sentences.t:
Aurea prima sata est aetas, quae vindice nullo,
sponte sua, sine lege fidem rectumque colebat.
sentences.l:
Golden and first was the age sown, which, with no avenger,
of its own accord, without law, cultivated faith and the right.
sentences.i: The golden age was the first to be sown — an age which, with nobody to enforce it, of its own accord and with no law, held to good faith and to what was right.
sentences.n: 'sata est' is from 'sero' (to sow): the age is sown like a crop, and 'prima' makes it the first of the four. 'vindice nullo' is an ablative absolute — 'with no avenger'; a 'vindex' at Rome was the man who stepped forward to claim or defend another at law, so the phrase means there was no call for legal redress. 'fidem rectumque': 'fides' is the Roman virtue of keeping one's word, the bond behind contracts and friendship; 'rectum' is the neuter adjective used as a noun, 'the straight thing'.

sentences.t:
Poena metusque aberant, nec verba minantia fixo
aere legebantur, nec supplex turba timebat
iudicis ora sui, sed erant sine vindice tuti.
sentences.l:
Punishment and fear were absent, nor were threatening words
read on fastened bronze, nor did a suppliant crowd dread
the face of its own judge, but they were safe without an avenger.
sentences.i: Punishment and fear were nowhere; no threatening words were read on bronze fastened up for all to see; no crowd of petitioners went in dread of the face of its own judge — they were safe, and needed no avenger to make them so.
sentences.n: 'verba minantia fixo aere' — the bronze on which laws were 'fixed' (fastened up) in the Forum, as the Twelve Tables were: the golden age is described by denying it the furniture of Ovid's own city. A 'iudex' was the private citizen appointed to hear a suit, so 'iudicis ora sui' is the face of the man before whom your own case falls. 'sine vindice tuti' picks up 'vindice nullo' from line 89 and closes the thought where it began.

sentences.t:
Nondum caesa suis, peregrinum ut viseret orbem,
montibus in liquidas pinus descenderat undas,
nullaque mortales praeter sua litora norant.
sentences.l:
Not yet, cut from its own mountains, so that it might see a foreign world,
had the pine come down into the flowing waves,
and mortals knew no shores but their own.
sentences.i: The pine had not yet been felled on its own mountains and come down to the flowing water to go and look at a foreign world; and men knew no shores but their own.
sentences.n: 'pinus' — the pine tree — stands for the ship built out of it, a metonymy Latin verse uses constantly; felling it and floating it is the first crossing of a boundary in this passage, and Ovid will come back to it at line 133. 'suis montibus' is ablative of separation with 'caesa', 'cut from its own mountains'; 'ut viseret' is a purpose clause with imperfect subjunctive, 'so that it might visit'. 'norant' is contracted from 'noverant' — 'they had come to know', hence simply 'they knew'.

sentences.i: No sheer moat yet ringed a town; there was no straight bronze trumpet, no curved bronze horn, no helmet and no sword:
sentences.n: 'aeris' (of bronze) is shared by both phrases and split between them — 'directi ... aeris' is the straight war-trumpet, 'flexi (aeris)' the curved horn, and the reader supplies the second 'aeris' from the first. Both are Roman army issue: the 'tuba' sounded the commands, the 'cornu' worked with the standards. 'erat' is singular though four things are being denied — the verb agrees with the nearest of them, 'ensis'.

sentences.t:
sine militis usu
mollia securae peragebant otia gentes.
sentences.l:
without any use for a soldier,
untroubled nations lived out a soft leisure.
sentences.n: 'otium' is the Roman word for leisure — time free of war and public business — and 'securae' is 'se-' + 'cura', 'free from care'. 'peragebant' ('were carrying through to the end') is imperfect, the tense that holds the golden age open as a lasting state rather than an event.

sentences.t:
ipsa quoque inmunis rastroque intacta nec ullis
saucia vomeribus per se dabat omnia tellus;
sentences.l:
she too, exempt from tribute and untouched by the hoe and by no
ploughshares wounded, of herself gave everything — the earth;
sentences.i: The earth too, exempt from all tribute, untouched by the hoe, wounded by no ploughshare, gave everything of her own accord;
sentences.n: The subject 'tellus' (earth) is held back to the last word, after all three things said about her — ordinary practice in Latin verse, and worth expecting. 'inmunis' is a tax word: a 'munus' is a duty or payment owed, so the earth is under no obligation and pays nothing. 'saucia' (wounded) makes the ploughshare a weapon — in this account tilling, like sailing and mining, is an injury done to the world.

sentences.t:
contentique cibis nullo cogente creatis
arbuteos fetus montanaque fraga legebant
cornaque et in duris haerentia mora rubetis
et quae deciderant patula Iovis arbore glandes.
sentences.l:
and content with foods brought forth with nothing forcing them,
they gathered the arbutus's fruit and mountain strawberries
and cornel-cherries and blackberries clinging in the hard brambles
and the acorns that had fallen from Jupiter's spreading tree.
sentences.n: 'nullo cogente' is another ablative absolute — 'with nothing compelling' — and it states the whole principle of the age: nothing has to be made to happen. 'legebant' is 'they gathered': 'lego' is to pick up or collect, and 'to read' is a further sense of the same verb, which is how it turned up as 'legebantur' in line 92. 'Iovis arbore' is the oak, sacred to Jupiter; a diet of acorns is the standard picture of the earliest men.

sentences.t:
Ver erat aeternum, placidique tepentibus auris
mulcebant zephyri natos sine semine flores.
sentences.l:
Spring was everlasting, and with warm breezes the gentle
west winds stroked flowers born without seed.
sentences.n: 'zephyri' are the west winds, which in Greek and Roman poetry bring the spring; 'tepentibus auris' is ablative of means, 'with their warming breezes'. 'natos sine semine' (born without seed) is the golden age in miniature, and matches the earth of line 102 that needs no plough.

sentences.t:
Mox etiam fruges tellus inarata ferebat,
nec renovatus ager gravidis canebat aristis;
sentences.l:
Soon the earth, unploughed, bore grain as well,
and the field, not turned afresh, whitened with heavy ears;
sentences.i: Before long the unploughed earth bore grain as well, and a field never broken up again went white with heavy ears;
sentences.n: 'nec' here negates the participle rather than the verb: 'nec renovatus ager' is 'the field not renewed', i.e. never left fallow and turned again, as Roman farming required. 'canebat' is 'grew white, went hoary' — the colour of ripe grain. 'inarata' is 'in-' (not) + 'aratus' (ploughed), a negative compound of the kind Latin verse forms freely.

sentences.t:
flumina iam lactis, iam flumina nectaris ibant,
flavaque de viridi stillabant ilice mella.
sentences.l:
rivers now of milk, now rivers of nectar ran,
and golden honey dripped from the green holm-oak.
sentences.n: 'iam ... iam' is 'now ... now', marking two things side by side rather than two moments. 'nectar' is the gods' own drink: in this age the earth puts out what belongs to heaven. 'mella' is a plural used of a single substance, normal in verse; the 'ilex' is the evergreen holm-oak, and honey was thought to fall on the leaves like dew.

sentences.t:
Postquam, Saturno tenebrosa in Tartara misso,
sub Iove mundus erat, subiit argentea proles,
auro deterior, fulvo pretiosior aere.
sentences.l:
After — Saturn having been sent into shadowy Tartarus —
the world was under Jove, the silver race came in beneath,
worse than gold, more precious than tawny bronze.
sentences.i: After Saturn had been cast into shadowy Tartarus and the world stood under Jove, the silver race came in, inferior to gold, more precious than tawny bronze.
sentences.n: 'Saturno ... misso' is an ablative absolute — 'with Saturn sent away'. Saturn ruled the golden age until his son Jupiter deposed him; the Romans identified him with an old Italian god of sowing and kept his festival, the Saturnalia, as a yearly memory of that reign. 'Tartara' (neuter plural) is the pit below the underworld where the beaten Titans are held — not the ordinary land of the dead. 'subiit' means both 'came next' and 'came in underneath', which is exactly how one age slips in below another here.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter antiqui contraxit tempora veris
perque hiemes aestusque et inaequalis autumnos
et breve ver spatiis exegit quattuor annum.
sentences.l:
Jupiter drew in the span of the ancient spring
and through winters and heats and unequal autumns
and a short spring drove the year through in four stretches.
sentences.i: Jupiter shortened the old spring, and drove the year through four spans — winters, and heats, and unequal autumns, and a brief spring.
sentences.n: 'contraxit' is 'drew together, pulled in' — the verb used of taking in sail. 'exegit ... annum' is 'drove the year through to its end' (ex + ago), and 'spatiis quattuor' is ablative, 'in four stretches', a 'spatium' being the course a runner or chariot covers. 'inaequalis' is the accusative plural in '-is' for '-es', common in verse; the 'unequal' autumns are the season whose weather will not settle.

sentences.t:
Tum primum siccis aer fervoribus ustus
canduit, et ventis glacies adstricta pependit.
sentences.l:
Then first the air, scorched by dry burnings,
glowed white, and ice, drawn tight by the winds, hung.
sentences.i: Then for the first time the air, scorched by dry heat, glowed white, and ice, bound hard by the winds, hung down.
sentences.n: 'siccis fervoribus' is ablative of means with 'ustus' ('burnt'); 'canduit' is to be white-hot, the word for metal in the fire. 'adstricta' ('drawn tight, bound fast') is what winter does to water — the ice here is icicles, hanging. 'Tum primum' will open three sentences running: Ovid is listing the world's first winter, first houses, first ploughing.

sentences.t:
Tum primum subiere domus (domus antra fuerunt
et densi frutices et vinctae cortice virgae).
sentences.l:
Then first they went in under houses (the houses were caves
and thick shrubs and rods bound with bark).
sentences.i: Then for the first time men went in under a roof — and the roofs were caves, dense thickets, branches lashed with bark.
sentences.n: 'subiere' is the poetic third-person plural perfect for 'subierunt' — the '-ēre' ending you meet everywhere in verse (compare 'gemuere' two lines on, 'fugere' at 129). 'subire domus' is literally 'to go in under houses', with the accusative of the thing gone under. 'vinctae cortice virgae' — rods bound with bark — is wattle-work, the beginning of building; 'cortice' is ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Semina tum primum longis Cerealia sulcis
obruta sunt, pressique iugo gemuere iuvenci.
sentences.l:
Then first the seeds of Ceres were buried in long furrows,
and bullocks, pressed by the yoke, groaned.
sentences.i: Then for the first time the seed of Ceres was buried in long furrows, and young oxen groaned under the press of the yoke.
sentences.n: 'Cerealia semina' is grain, named from Ceres the goddess of the crops — Latin poetry regularly names the god for the thing. 'gemuere' is the '-ēre' perfect again (= 'gemuerunt'). 'pressi iugo' (pressed by the yoke) puts the cost of agriculture into the animals' mouths: the silver age gets bread, and something has to carry it.

sentences.t:
Tertia post illam successit aenea proles,
saevior ingeniis et ad horrida promptior arma,
non scelerata tamen.
sentences.l:
Third after that one came the bronze race,
fiercer in its temper and readier for bristling arms,
yet not criminal.
sentences.i: Third after that one came the race of bronze, harsher in temper and quicker to reach for grim weapons — not wicked, though.
sentences.n: 'aenea' is 'of bronze' ('aes'), the metal of Roman arms and armour before iron and the metal of the war-trumpet back at line 98: naming the age is enough to say what it is for. 'saevior ... promptior' are comparatives measured against the silver race just described, and 'ingeniis' is ablative of respect, 'in their inborn natures'. 'scelerata' comes back six lines on in 'amor sceleratus habendi' (131), of the iron age: a 'scelus' is a crime against what is owed to gods and kin.

sentences.t:
De duro est ultima ferro.
Protinus inrupit venae peioris in aevum
omne nefas:
sentences.l:
The last is of hard iron.
At once into the age of the baser vein burst
every unspeakable thing:
sentences.i: The last age is of hard iron. Straightway into that age of baser ore every abomination broke in:
sentences.n: Supply 'aetas' with 'ultima' — 'the last (age) is of hard iron'. Iron is the metal of the plough and of the sword, cheap and hard and thoroughly Roman, and the present tenses that follow put this age in the reader's own day. 'venae peioris' is a genitive describing the age — 'of a worse vein', a 'vena' being the seam of metal in the rock, so the age is named from its ore. 'nefas' is the strongest word available: not merely a crime but the thing that is 'not right' in the eyes of the gods and not to be spoken; 'inrupit' is the verb for a wall being breached.

sentences.i: shame fled, and truth, and good faith; and into their place came cheating and trickery and ambush and violence and the wicked love of getting.
sentences.n: 'fugere' is not the infinitive here but the '-ēre' perfect, 'they fled' (= 'fugerunt') — the tell is that 'pudor', 'verum' and 'fides' are nominatives, so the verb needs a plural subject. 'in quorum locum' is a connecting relative opening the sentence: 'and into their place'. 'amor habendi' is 'love of having', a gerund in the genitive, and 'sceleratus' finally lands the word withheld from the bronze race. 'pudor' is the sense of shame that keeps a Roman from acting badly in front of others; with it and 'fides' gone, the list that follows is what fills the vacancy.

sentences.t:
Vela dabat ventis (nec adhuc bene noverat illos)
navita; quaeque diu steterant in montibus altis,
fluctibus ignotis insultavere carinae,
sentences.l:
He was giving sails to the winds (and did not yet know them well) —
the sailor; and the keels which had long stood on high mountains
leapt upon waters they did not know,
sentences.i: The sailor was spreading his sails to winds he still knew little of; and keels that had long stood on high mountains now danced on waters they had never known,
sentences.n: The subject 'navita' (sailor) is held past the line-end and lands after the parenthesis — the delay is the point: he is already sailing before we are told who he is. 'quae ... carinae' is a relative clause with its noun kept inside it, so 'carinae' (keels, hence ships) arrives with the verb. 'insultavere' is the '-ēre' perfect of 'insulto' ('leap upon', built on 'salio', to leap), a verb also used of trampling on or exulting over something. This is the pine of line 95, now afloat.

sentences.t:
communemque prius ceu lumina solis et auras
cautus humum longo signavit limite mensor.
sentences.l:
and the ground, common before, like the light of the sun and the air,
the careful surveyor marked out with a long boundary-line.
sentences.i: and the land, common property until then, as sunlight and air are, the careful surveyor marked off with a long boundary-line.
sentences.n: The subject 'mensor' (measurer, land-surveyor) comes last again, and 'humum' is torn from its adjective 'communem' by the whole comparison — the line divides what it is describing. A 'limes' is the surveyed strip between fields, the basic unit of Roman land division, and 'longo limite' is ablative of means; land-surveying was a settled Roman profession with its own manuals. Sunlight and air are the standard examples of things nobody can own.

sentences.t:
Nec tantum segetes alimentaque debita dives
poscebatur humus, sed itum est in viscera terrae:
sentences.l:
Nor was the rich ground asked only for crops and the food it owed,
but men went into the entrails of the earth:
sentences.i: And the rich soil was not merely asked for crops and the food it owed; men went down into the earth's entrails:
sentences.n: 'poscebatur ... segetes' keeps the accusative of the thing demanded even though the verb is passive — the active 'posco' takes two accusatives ('posco te aliquid', I demand something of you). 'debita' ('owed') makes the harvest a debt the earth pays; what lies below the surface was never owed. 'itum est' is an impersonal passive of 'eo' — literally 'it was gone', i.e. 'men went'; Latin can make even an intransitive verb passive this way. 'viscera' are the inner organs, so the mining is a disembowelling.

sentences.t:
quasque recondiderat Stygiisque admoverat umbris,
effodiuntur opes, inritamenta malorum.
sentences.l:
and the riches which she had hidden away and moved close to the Stygian shades
are dug out — the goads of evils.
sentences.i: and the wealth she had buried away and set close beside the shades of Styx is dug up — the goad of every evil.
sentences.n: 'quas ... opes' is a relative clause that runs ahead of its noun: 'the riches which she had hidden' — 'opes' waits and arrives with the main verb. The Styx is the underworld river, and the point is depth: the earth had put this metal as far from the living as the dead are. 'effodiuntur' switches into the present tense in mid-sentence, and the present then holds to the end of the age (prodit, vivitur, inminet, miscent): not a past made vivid, but the age the poem is speaking from. 'inritamenta' are things that provoke or incite: the gold does not merely accompany the evils, it starts them.

sentences.t:
Iamque nocens ferrum ferroque nocentius aurum
prodierat: prodit bellum, quod pugnat utroque,
sanguineaque manu crepitantia concutit arma.
sentences.l:
And by now harmful iron, and gold more harmful than iron,
had come forth; war comes forth, which fights with both,
and shakes clattering arms with a bloody hand.
sentences.i: And by now hurtful iron had come to light, and gold more hurtful than iron; and out comes war, which fights with both, and rattles its clashing weapons with a bloodstained hand.
sentences.n: 'prodierat ... prodit' is the same verb twice over, pluperfect then present: the metals 'had come forth' out of the ground, and war 'comes forth' after them, as though it were the third thing mined. 'nocentius' is the comparative of the participle 'nocens' ('doing harm'). 'utroque' is ablative of 'uterque', 'with both of them' — iron and gold, the sword and what pays for it.

sentences.t:
Vivitur ex rapto: non hospes ab hospite tutus,
non socer a genero; fratrum quoque gratia rara est.
sentences.l:
Living is done from what has been snatched: a guest is not safe from his host,
nor a father-in-law from his son-in-law; goodwill between brothers, too, is rare.
sentences.i: Men live off what they can seize: a guest is not safe from his host, nor a father-in-law from the man who married his daughter; even goodwill between brothers is rare.
sentences.n: 'vivitur' is another impersonal passive — 'it is lived', i.e. 'people live' (compare 'itum est' six lines back); 'ex rapto' is a neuter participle used as a noun, 'from what has been seized'. 'hospes' means both host and guest: one word covers both sides of the bond of hospitality, which is what makes the line sting. Each pair Ovid names is a tie of obligation — guest and host, marriage-alliance, blood kinship — and 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'also', not the 'quō-que' ('and with which') it can be elsewhere.

sentences.i: A husband hangs over his wife's death, she over her husband's; dread stepmothers mix the livid aconite; the son asks after his father's years before their time.
sentences.n: 'inminet' ('leans over, threatens') takes the dative of the thing threatened, 'exitio', and 'coniugis' is a genitive depending on it — 'over the destruction of his wife'. 'aconitum' is monkshood, the standard poison of Roman rhetoric, and the wicked 'noverca' (stepmother) is its standard dispenser. 'ante diem ... inquirit in annos' — he enquires into his father's years before the day: he is reckoning how long the old man has left, which is to say wanting the inheritance early; 'ante diem' is the phrase for anything that arrives before its appointed time.

sentences.t:
Victa iacet pietas, et virgo caede madentis,
ultima caelestum terras Astraea reliquit.
sentences.l:
Conquered, piety lies low; and the maiden Astraea,
last of the heaven-dwellers, left the lands soaked with slaughter.
sentences.i: Piety lies beaten; and the maiden Astraea, last of the gods to go, left an earth soaked in slaughter.
sentences.n: 'madentis' is the accusative plural in '-is' (for '-es') agreeing with 'terras' — 'the lands dripping' — and it is split from its noun across the line-break. 'pietas' is the virtue that holds this whole stretch together: the duty owed to gods, parents, kin and country, the quality that makes Virgil's Aeneas 'pius'; the crimes just listed are what it looks like when that duty fails. Astraea is Justice, the starry maiden, who lived among men in the golden age and withdrew to the sky as they worsened — 'ultima caelestum', the last of the gods to give up on the earth.

sentences.t:
Neve foret terris securior arduus aether,
adfectasse ferunt regnum caeleste Gigantas
altaque congestos struxisse ad sidera montes.
sentences.l:
And lest the steep upper air be safer than the lands,
they say the Giants made an attempt on the kingdom of heaven
and built mountains, heaped one on another, up to the high stars.
sentences.i: And so that the steep air above should be no safer than the earth below, the Giants — so the story goes — made an attempt on the kingdom of heaven and piled mountains up towards the high stars.
sentences.n: 'ferunt' ('they say, the story goes') with the accusative-and-infinitive is how Latin reports a legend at arm's length: 'adfectasse ... Gigantas' = 'that the Giants attempted'. 'adfectasse' is contracted from 'adfectavisse', and 'adfecto' is to reach for what is not yours — the verb used of grasping at a throne. The Giants were the huge sons of Earth who rose against the gods; the mountain-piling is told in Homer of the brothers Otus and Ephialtes (Odyssey 11), and Latin poetry regularly folds it into the Giants' assault, as Ovid does here, assuming the story rather than telling it. 'Gigantas' keeps its Greek accusative plural ending, as Greek names in Latin verse often do.

sentences.t:
Tum pater omnipotens misso perfregit Olympum
fulmine et excussit subiectae Pelion Ossae.
sentences.l:
Then the almighty father, with a thunderbolt sent,
shattered Olympus and struck Pelion off Ossa beneath it.
sentences.i: Then the almighty father loosed his bolt, shattered Olympus, and knocked Pelion off Ossa underneath.
sentences.n: 'misso ... fulmine' is an ablative absolute split across the line-break — 'with his thunderbolt loosed'. 'pater omnipotens' is the formal epic title of Jupiter, familiar from Virgil. The mountains are the pile itself, real peaks of Thessaly: in the usual version Ossa goes on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa, so 'excussit subiectae Pelion Ossae' is 'shook Pelion off Ossa lying underneath', with 'Ossae' a dative of separation.

sentences.t:
Obruta mole sua cum corpora dira iacerent,
perfusam multo natorum sanguine Terram
inmaduisse ferunt calidumque animasse cruorem,
sentences.l:
When their dreadful bodies lay buried under their own mass,
they say that Earth, drenched with the abundant blood of her sons,
was soaked through and gave life to the warm gore,
sentences.i: When those monstrous bodies lay crushed beneath the very mass they had piled up, Earth — so the story goes — was drenched with her sons' blood, soaked it up, and put life into the warm gore,
sentences.n: 'cum ... iacerent' is circumstantial 'cum' with the imperfect subjunctive, 'when they lay'. 'mole sua' is the heap of mountains they piled themselves, now their grave — ablative with 'obruta', 'buried under their own mass'. 'ferunt' again governs accusative-and-infinitive: 'Terram inmaduisse ... animasse' ('that Earth grew soaked and gave life'), with 'animasse' contracted from 'animavisse'. The Giants are Earth's children ('natorum'), which is why the blood soaks into a mother.

sentences.t:
et, ne nulla suae stirpis monimenta manerent,
in faciem vertisse hominum.
sentences.l:
and, lest no memorials of her own stock should remain,
that she turned it into the shape of men.
sentences.i: and — so that some memorial of her own line should survive — turned it into the shape of men.
sentences.n: 'ne nulla ... manerent' is a double negative used positively: 'lest no memorials remain' means 'so that some memorial should remain'. 'vertisse' continues the string of infinitives depending on 'ferunt' in the previous line. 'stirps' is stock or lineage (first the root of a plant, then of a family) and 'monimenta' are things that keep a memory alive: this new human race is Earth's monument to her dead sons.

sentences.t:
Sed et illa propago
contemptrix superum saevaeque avidissima caedis
et violenta fuit: scires e sanguine natos.
sentences.l:
But that offspring too was a despiser of the gods above
and most greedy of savage slaughter
and violent: you would know they were born from blood.
sentences.i: But that brood too was a despiser of the gods, greedy beyond measure for savage bloodshed, and violent: you would have known them born of blood.
sentences.n: 'contemptrix' is the feminine agent-noun ('she who despises') agreeing with 'propago', and it governs 'superum' — the shortened genitive plural of 'superi', 'those above', the gods. 'avidissima caedis' takes the genitive after the superlative adjective, 'greediest for slaughter'. 'scires' is a potential subjunctive addressed to the reader — 'you would know' — and the inference is left to be drawn rather than stated.
